Concept 05

Distributed processing

The same Pipeline, run by several processes at once against different slices of the same data. Coordination is a lease on a row range; durability is Arrow IPC bytes in a raft-replicated redb file.

In one line
Many nodes, one pipeline, at-least-once per row range
You need
saci-service with distributed, which needs no external service; add distributed-raft for a cluster
Read this if
One process is not enough, and you need work to survive a node dying halfway through a batch

The claim loop

DistributedRunner holds three things: a store, a Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> used as a template, and a RunnerConfig. Calling run(world_factory) starts a loop that claims work, runs the template against it, persists the result, and acknowledges. Then it goes back for more, until the store says there is nothing pending.

PartitionSource::claim_next_batch hands back a BatchClaim: a batch_id, a half-open Range<u32> of rows, a fresh claim_id, and a lease that expires at a wall-clock millisecond. Hold the lease and the range is yours. Lose it and somebody else gets the same rows.

claims, leases, coordination rows and Arrow IPC bytes

Two lease mechanisms keep the window narrow. Before the run, should_renew checks whether less than 30 % of the TTL (or ten seconds, whichever is smaller) remains, and renews if so. During the run a renewal task sits beside run_on_with_state in the same tokio::select!, renewing at TTL/3. If a renewal fails the select resolves on the renewal branch, the run is cancelled at its next await point, and the claim is released rather than acked. A runner never keeps working on a lease it has lost.

The same is true after the run. If the checkpoint write fails, or the accumulator save fails, or the state blob save fails, the runner calls release_claim and skips the ack. Nothing is acknowledged that could not be made durable.

Those two rules add up to at-least-once delivery. A claim, its holder and its expiry are one raft log entry, so every node reads the same claim state. RedbSharedStore grants each claim a 90 s lease of its own. A saci-service cluster config overrides that with lease_ttl_ms, which defaults to 30 s. A running node proposes an expiry sweep every 30 s, which returns an expired range to pending for another node to claim.

An ack is issued only after the processor run and the checkpoint write both complete, so a SIGKILL mid-claim loses no data. The lease expires and another node reclaims the range. Processing pauses by up to one lease plus one sweep interval for any range in flight at kill time.

The runner does not load your rows

world_factory is called once per claim and whatever it returns is what the pipeline sees. The runner never reads the master batch's Arrow IPC back out of the store. Registering the components and filling in the rows for claim.row_range is your closure's job. See examples/distributed_fulfillment/store.rs, which wraps the store to intercept claim_next_batch and stash the IPC where the factory can reach it.

Standalone and clustered

Both modes use the same two traits, the same runner and the same RedbSharedStore. Standalone applies each mutation straight to its local redb file. Clustering proposes the identical mutation through raft, so every node applies it in the same order.

FeatureWhat it adds
distributed PartitionSource, CheckpointStore, DistributedRunner, CheckpointStrategy and RedbSharedStore::single_node. It carries redb, so one node needs no external service.
distributed-raft The SACI raft node, on openraft: ArrowRedbLogStore over raft-log.redb, ArrowRedbStateMachine over cluster-app.redb, ArrowRaftDriver, the TCP peer transport, and RedbSharedStore::multi_node. Implies distributed.
service-cluster service plus distributed-raft: what the saci-service binary needs to run mode "cluster" from a config file. Add the connectors and the wasm or plugin feature the config names, and nothing else: a cluster node's state is the cluster-app.redb under node.data_dir.

A claim is a raft proposal, and the state machine rejects a range that overlaps a claimed or completed one, so the log order arbitrates. Every mutation commits on the leader; reads go to the local replica. The three saci_raft_* gauges report the commit index, the term and the leader id.

Standalone persistence is a different file with a different job. A store "redb" block names one local, unreplicated redb file, and RedbStateClient keeps three things in it: the raw config bytes the service was started with, each processor's prior, and each source's cursor. It carries no batches, no claims and no checkpoints, which is why cluster mode has no use for it and refuses the block. Its keys are on Run modes and persistence.

Publishing work

A master batch is a registered chunk of Arrow IPC with an id, a component name, a schema version, and a row count. Runners never create batches; they consume them.

Rustfive arguments, in this order
store
    .register_master_batch(
        0,                         // batch_id: u64
        Order::name().to_string(), // component: String
        1,                         // schema_id: u32
        ipc_bytes,                 // Vec<u8>, an Arrow IPC stream
        900,                       // total_rows: u32
    )
    .await?;

Registration is what creates the work. register_master_batch proposes one RegisterMasterBatch command, and the state machine writes the record into arrow_master_batches and marks the id in arrow_pending_batches. Row ranges are not pre-cut. A claim carves the first uncovered span off the batch when it is granted. Parallelism is therefore a function of how many batches you register.

claim_next_batch walks arrow_pending_batches, then reads that batch's claims out of the arrow_claims_by_batch index in row order and returns the first span no claimed or completed range covers. Two nodes reaching the same span both propose it. The state machine commits one and answers the other with an overlap error, and the loser backs off and rescans, up to eight attempts.

One cap applies. MAX_LOG_ENTRY_BYTES is 1024 * 1024, because a payload travels inside a raft log entry. register_master_batch rejects an Arrow IPC payload that size or larger. The stage checkpoint, the window accumulator and the processor state blob all read the same number off CheckpointStore::max_checkpoint_bytes.

Running one node

One process against one local redb file is a real deployment, and the shortest path to seeing the loop work. It needs no external service, because the store is the file you name.

Rustfeatures = "distributed"
use std::path::Path;

use saci_service::SaciResult;
use saci_service::component::Component;
use saci_service::dataset::Dataset;
use saci_service::distributed::RedbSharedStore;
use saci_service::distributed::runner::{DistributedRunner, RunnerConfig};
use saci_service::distributed::strategy::CheckpointStrategy;
use saci_service::pipeline::Pipeline;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> SaciResult<()> {
    // One file holds the batches, the claims and the checkpoints. Two
    // deployments stay apart by naming different files.
    let store = RedbSharedStore::single_node(Path::new("/var/lib/saci/shared.redb"))?;

    let (ipc_bytes, total_rows) = encode_orders_ipc()?;
    store
        .register_master_batch(0, Order::name().to_string(), 1, ipc_bytes, total_rows)
        .await?;

    // A template. Its own dataset, sources and sinks are never used: each
    // claim runs against whatever `world_factory` hands back.
    let template = Pipeline::builder("order-processor")
        .with::<Order>()
        .with_system(ValidateOrder)
        .with_system(PriceOrder)
        .build();

    let runner = DistributedRunner::new(
        store,
        Box::new(template),
        RunnerConfig {
            checkpoint_strategy: CheckpointStrategy::EveryStage,
            schema_id: 1,
            max_batches: None,
            ..Default::default()
        },
    );

    // Called once per claim. Register the components and load the rows here.
    let processed = runner.run(hydrate_partition).await?;
    println!("{processed} batches acked");
    Ok(())
}

run returns the number of batches it acked. It stops when claim_next_batch returns None, or when max_batches is reached. For a long-lived service use run_with_shutdown, which takes a CancellationToken and exits between batches without holding a lease.

Two examples run this loop end to end against a fresh redb file in the temporary directory, so nothing has to be running beside them.

Shellruns the same on Linux, macOS and Windows (PowerShell)
cargo run -p saci-service --example distributed_scheduler --features distributed
cargo run -p saci-service --example distributed_windowed --features distributed,windows

Where state lives

A cluster node's data_dir holds four files and nothing else. raft-log.redb is this node's raft log. cluster-app.redb is the replicated application state. Every node applies the same committed entries in the same order, so every node ends with the same copy. bootstrap.lock and node-id are one line each.

the raft log and its traffic the replicated application state

All three checkpoint kinds share one key space and one API. They are told apart by stage_idx, and the two reserved values sit far above any real stage index, which numbers from zero and stays in the dozens.

ConstantValuePayload
none 0 The whole partition Dataset, written by the runner after the run.
PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX - 1 Whatever run_on_with_state returned. Opaque to the host.
ACCUMULATOR_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX The WindowAccumulator component alone, via write_component_ipc.
The stage checkpoint is write-only, and there is one of it

The runner calls run_on_with_state once per claim, since the runtime runs its own stages internally, then writes a single checkpoint at stage_idx = 0. Nothing reads it back, because recovery re-runs the batch from the top rather than resuming mid-pipeline. Two consequences. CheckpointStrategy::EveryNStages(n) only ever fires for n == 1, because the sole call is should_checkpoint(0). And the checkpoint is an artefact for an operator or an external reader, not a resume point.

Wiring a cluster

A cluster node runs two things side by side: a raft driver that replicates the application state, and a store that proposes into it. ArrowRaftDriver::start is async, takes the raft log path and the application database path, and returns the handle plus the driver's task. Keep the task alive for the life of the process.

Rustfeatures = "distributed-raft"
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Arc;

use saci_service::distributed::RedbSharedStore;
use saci_service::distributed::consensus::{ArrowRaftDriver, ArrowRaftDriverConfig};

let (handle, _driver_task) = ArrowRaftDriver::start(
    ArrowRaftDriverConfig {
        node_id: 1,
        listen_addr: "0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap(),
        // "host:port" strings, resolved lazily at connect time, so Docker
        // service names work. An empty map auto-initialises a single node.
        peers: HashMap::from([
            (2, "saci-2:9001".to_string()),
            (3, "saci-3:9001".to_string()),
        ]),
        heartbeat_interval_ms: 300,
        election_timeout_min_ms: 1_500,
        election_timeout_max_ms: 3_000,
    },
    data_dir.join("raft-log.redb"),      // this node's log
    data_dir.join("cluster-app.redb"),   // this node's copy of the state
)
.await?;

// `start` wires outbound connections only. Without this listener peers cannot
// deliver votes, heartbeats or log entries, and no leader is ever elected.
let _tcp_server = handle.spawn_tcp_server("0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap()).await?;

// The store proposes through the driver and reads the same database the state
// machine writes, so it opens no second file handle.
let store = RedbSharedStore::multi_node(Arc::clone(handle.app_db()), handle.clone());

From here the runner code is byte-for-byte the single-node code: same template, same RunnerConfig, same runner.run(...). Only the driver is new.

Membership is explicit. bootstrap #true on one node calls initialize with the configured peer set and then writes bootstrap.lock. The file records that this cluster was deliberately created, and stops a later start from doing it twice. Every other node starts with bootstrap #false and is caught up by the leader.

You do not route work to the leader, but every mutation ends up there. RedbSharedStore proposes each command with Raft::client_write. On a follower that call returns ForwardToLeader, and the store then sends the same command to the leader's configured address over the length-prefixed TCP transport the peers already use. Reads never leave the node, and open the local cluster-app.redb directly. A propose made while no leader is elected comes back as a retryable error, and one that reaches a leader but never commits times out after 30 seconds. The saci-service binary does all of the wiring above from a config file under mode "cluster", so hand-rolling it is only for embedding the runner in your own process.

Payload caps

Three constants bound what one proposal, one snapshot chunk and one peer frame may carry.

CapValueWhat it bounds
MAX_LOG_ENTRY_BYTES 1 MiB The Arrow IPC payload of a registered master batch, and, as the CheckpointStore::max_checkpoint_bytes default, of one stage checkpoint. In src/distributed/partition.rs.
SNAPSHOT_CHUNK_BYTES 4 MiB One chunk of a state-machine snapshot. In src/distributed/consensus/transport/mod.rs.
MAX_FRAME_BYTES 16 MiB One length-prefixed TCP frame on the peer transport, which carries raft messages, forwarded proposals and snapshot chunks. Same file.

If registration rejects a batch, split the input across several batch_ids rather than raising the constant. A claim covers the pending row range of one batch, so several smaller batches are also what spreads work across nodes.

Checkpoint strategies

Checkpoint strategy is set on DistributedRunner, in code rather than config. The default is EveryStage.

StrategyBehaviourUse when
EveryStage Checkpoint after every pipeline stage Maximum recovery granularity; highest write amplification
EveryNStages(n) Checkpoint every N stages Balance durability and write cost
None No checkpointing Idempotent pipelines that can safely re-run from the start

For long pipelines with expensive stages, EveryNStages reduces how much each batch writes into the raft log.

State that outlives a batch

A native Pipeline keeps everything it knows in the Dataset, so the default run_on_with_state ignores prior, delegates to run_on, and returns Ok(None). Nothing extra is persisted.

A WASM processor cannot do that. Every call gets a fresh wasmtime Store, so processor linear memory does not survive a batch. That is deliberate, because a trapped instance cannot corrupt anything that outlives it. The one channel left is the return value:

Rustthe host seam, from saci-core
async fn run_on_with_state(
    &self,
    data: &mut Dataset,
    prior: Option<&[u8]>,
) -> SaciResult<Option<Vec<u8>>>;

WasmPipelineRuntime passes prior straight into the processor's run-batch export and returns the checkpoint field of the result. The runner stores that blob under PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL and hands it back as the next call's prior. On the processor side, one macro form opts in:

Rustin the processor crate
// Stateless: `prior` is ignored, `checkpoint` is always None.
saci_processor::export_pipeline!(build);

// Stateful: systems read and write a `ProcessorState<Counter>` resource, and
// whatever they leave in it becomes the next batch's `prior`.
saci_processor::export_pipeline!(build, state = Counter);

The pointer to the newest blob is a chain, not a fixed key. The blob is written under the claim that produced it and read back under the id of the claim that wrote the previous one. The state machine resolves a checkpoint's batch_id through the claims table, and rejects a write whose uuid names no claim. Reads survive the ack, so the chain holds for as long as the runner loop does. A runner that restarts hands the runtime None, so the processor starts cold and rebuilds its state.
